item.description: Warming water does not just move fish around; it pulls the whole food web out from under the birds that depend on it. Common murres pushed to their limits during heatwaves end up washing ashore emaciated, and that is a warning written in seabirds rathe... Ver más metapodcast Fuente: National Geographic.

item.title: Laser-plasma accelerator could generate bright X-rays for biological imaging, simulations show
item.description: X-rays with wavelengths between approximately 2.3 and 4.4 nanometers, i.e., in the so-called water window, are particularly well suited to examining biological samples in their natural, aqueous environment. To date, however, it has been technically difficult to access this type of radiation at an appropriate quality and intensity, as only free-electron lasers in large-scale accelerator systems are capable of generating it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Land plants' closest algal relatives evolved multicellular growth repeatedly, genetic analysis suggests
item.description: What did the algae that gave rise to the first land plants look like? A research team led by the University of Göttingen and including the universities of Maastricht and Innsbruck and Museo Nacional de Ciencias Naturales has now taken a detailed look at one of the most important groups for answering this question: the Zygnematophyceae, the closest living algal relatives of land plants. These include familiar-looking filamentous algae such as Spirogyra, as well as many that just consist of single cells. Despite their relatively simple appearance, they are particularly important for… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Paired DNA strands recognize shape, not just sequence, in new small-molecule sensing method
item.description: You have probably performed a sandwich assay before, even if you didn't know it. Sandwich assays are the molecular sensing technology behind lateral flow tests like the at-home COVID test. After a sample is dripped onto the test strip, it combines with detector antibodies attached to tiny gold particles, which bind to any viral proteins present. When the sample reaches the test line, a second antibody anchored to the strip binds to a different site on the viral protein, creating a molecular "sandwich." As the gold particles accumulate, the test line turns dark red, becoming visible to the… Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Underwater cameras can estimate fish weight in real time without generating full depth maps
item.description: Accurate fish-weight estimates can help aquaculture operators manage feeding, monitor growth and plan harvests. However, conventional underwater imaging methods often require substantial computing power and can struggle with reflections, bubbles and turbid water. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New placenta-on-a-chip model allows engineers to study effects of environmental toxins
item.description: Exposure to toxic metals like cadmium has been associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes such as miscarriage, preterm birth and low birth weight. Because these effects are difficult and ethically challenging to study directly in pregnant women, how such exposures affect pregnancy has remained poorly understood. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: France's shorter workweek hit lower-skilled workers harder
item.description: Doing more with less has become standard operating procedure for many in the current economic climate. And for some in the wake of France's 1998 workweek reduction, it was in response to a reform that's still being debated today. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Antibiotic pollution may be key factor in honeybee colony collapses
item.description: High losses of honeybee colonies, which play a crucial role in global food production, have caused concern around the world. Many potential factors for the population declines have been cited, but a potentially significant threat to pollinator health—environmental antibiotic pollution from agricultural sources—has been largely overlooked, according to a new article published in the Journal of the American Veterinary Medical Association. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Construyen el puente para animales más grande del mundo, una obra que busca reconectar hábitats y proteger a pumas aislados
item.description: California ultima los detalles del Wallis Annenberg Wildlife Crossing en Agoura Hills; la megaestructura vial facilita el tránsito seguro de especies amenazadas y combate la endogamia genética en los felinos Fuente: La Nación - El Mundo.

item.title: Pinning down the structure of quark-gluon plasma, the universe's first fluid
item.description: In the first fraction of a second following the Big Bang, matter existed as a trillion-degree plasma of quarks and gluons—subatomic particles that zinged around at close to the speed of light. This roiling soup lasted for just a few microseconds before the particles coalesced into more stable protons and neutrons. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What AI can lose when it makes Holocaust writings easier to read
item.description: In an Amsterdam prison during the Nazi occupation, Sal Bramson drew his cell on pieces of cotton cloth. He added handwritten explanations and sent these messages to his mother, concealed inside a shirt collar among the prison laundry. The cloth could travel because it passed as something ordinary. Its material was part of what made communication possible. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research explores how offshore wind development may alter marine food webs
item.description: As offshore wind development expands along the U.S. Atlantic Coast, understanding its potential effects on marine ecosystems is increasingly important. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA unveils mysterious X-70 experimental aircraft using AI-generated image
item.description: NASA’s X-70 Fractal announcement comes as agency aims to grow X-plane fleet. Fuente: Ars Technica.
item.dc:creator: Jeremy Hsu

item.title: Leaf nutrient balance helps explain earlier fall color in US forests
item.description: For devout leaf peepers, timing is everything. A new study led by researchers from Duke University's Nicholas School of the Environment shows that leaf nutrient levels affect the onset of fall color. The findings, published in Nature Communications, could improve leaf drop forecasts and carbon cycle tracking. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New research explores what our appetite for a digital detox can tell us
item.description: How we feel about taking a break from our screens could tell us something important about the way we behave online, according to new research from the University of Bath and Goethe University Frankfurt. Researchers have developed the first validated scale specifically designed to measure people's attitudes toward temporarily reducing their digital consumption, finding considerable differences in how positively people view the prospect of switching off. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New tests expand empathy measurement to joyful stories and embarrassing mishaps
item.description: Listening to someone recount their visit to an amusement park can feel like being on an emotional roller coaster yourself. Even if the listeners have never set foot in the park, they can still empathize with the other person's feelings: the deep disappointment when it turns out that their favorite ride is closed. The joy—at having the best ice cream of their life. And the embarrassment—after that ice cream abruptly left their stomach on the Freefall Tower. Put simply: whatever the other person is feeling, we feel it with them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Researchers call for rethink on disposal of washed-up whale carcasses
item.description: Marine scientist Olaf Meynecke says disposing of dead whales is complex, costly and should not fall to local councils. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Gabrielle Becerra Mellet

item.title: Black characters receive similar precision ratings whether they look 'nerdy' or 'chill'
item.description: People are often asked simple questions, such as the price of the cheapest flight to a particular destination. But the answers—and how they are perceived—can reveal far more than the cost of that trip itself. For example, whether a person believes that the response "It's $200" means $200 or assumes that the figure has been rounded up or down depends on their perception of the person giving the answer. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Connecting artificial intelligence with the tools of astrophysical research
item.description: Investigating a scientific question is often a complex process. As an astrophysicist studying some of the most energetic phenomena in the universe, I know that finding answers requires much more than reading scientific papers or understanding existing theories. Astrophysical research involves collecting observations, analyzing data, building physical models and comparing their predictions with observations. These tasks require different scientific tools, databases and modeling software and can take considerable time even for experienced researchers. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Electrical control of an unconventional quantum transport state demonstrated in a magnet for the first time
item.description: Researchers at Tohoku University and the Japan Atomic Energy Agency (JAEA) have successfully controlled a unique quantum phenomenon—the quantum-geometric nonlinear Hall (QgNLH) state—using electric current for the first time. The breakthrough was achieved by revealing and exploiting the coupling between the spin structure and the QgNLH state in an electrically switchable chiral antiferromagnet. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How palm orientation shapes spin characteristics in volleyball jump serves
item.description: A new biomechanical study has uncovered how elite volleyball players control ball spin during jump serves, offering fresh scientific insight into one of the sport's most decisive offensive skills. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Physicist develops detector capable of counting photons for quantum computing
item.description: Detecting a single photon is a challenge in itself. But what if you also want to know exactly how many photons arrive at a particular point at the same time? Physicist Erik Baalbergen is working on light detectors that can do just that. They form a key building block for the optical quantum computer of the future. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: As Antarctic blue whales advance along the road to recovery, continued oversight is key
item.description: Antarctic blue whales appear to be creeping back from the brink of extinction after 50 years of protection. A new study estimates the total population at 4,018, up from 418 after the last reported whale catch in 1973. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How octopuses squeeze through too-small gaps
item.description: Octopuses are extraordinarily versatile. From walking across the seabed on their eight arms to jetting through the water, manipulating tools and squeezing through unimaginably tight spaces, the flexibility of octopuses almost defies belief. "Octopuses can change their body shape to squeeze through tiny holes, almost like water flowing through a gap, so their size doesn't always limit where they can go," says Wenci Xin from the National University of Singapore. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Blue Origin’s next launch now won’t happen until 2027
item.description: Blue Origin plans to do its next New Glenn rocket launch in January 2027, according to CNBC and the Financial Times, which cite a memo from CEO Dave Limp sent to staff. The new timeline follows a May launchpad explosion that damaged Blue Origin's New Glenn launchpad ahead of a flight that would have brought […] Fuente: The Verge.
item.dc:creator: Jay Peters

item.title: Born to be queen: A look inside fire ant hierarchy
item.description: A group of genes may give some fire ants an advantage, increasing their chances of growing larger and potentially becoming queens, according to a new study from the University of Georgia. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How private schools segregate students by class and strengthen social divisions
item.description: If you want to see how private schools in the U.K. can reinforce segregation between children of different social classes, the London Borough of Southwark provides a good example. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Newly identified protein mechanism helps explain how cells respond to physical forces
item.description: A newly published study is changing our understanding of how the protein talin functions at sites where cells attach to their surroundings. The findings uncover a previously unknown mechanism by which mechanical force regulates talin, a key protein controlling cell adhesion and mechanosensing. The paper is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Clothes on the bed, nothing feels right: The psychology behind your seasonal wardrobe meltdown
item.description: The clocks have gone back, and suddenly getting dressed feels more difficult. The coat you wore constantly last winter is still hanging in the closet, but it no longer looks quite how you remember. The boots you loved in February don't seem to go with anything, while a sweater that once felt like you somehow doesn't anymore. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hubble learns galactic history from stars
item.description: This NASA/ESA Hubble Space Telescope image provides a lesson in galactic history. The sparkling collection of stars is named Messier 30 (M30) after the French astronomer Charles Messier, who cataloged M30 and other diffuse objects that might be mistaken for comets in the early telescopes of Messier's time. M30 lies about 27,500 light-years away in the constellation Capricornus. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New microscopy method reveals tiny cell structures and their molecular surroundings
item.description: How do cells respond to drugs? A new microscopy technique could provide more precise answers to this question in the future. Researchers from Bielefeld University and the University of Vienna have developed a method as part of the European CHEM-SCAN project that makes the smallest cellular structures visible while also showing how their molecular environment changes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Hubble studied dwarf galaxies and found they kept just 11% of the oxygen made by their stars
item.description: A recent investigation revealed that dwarf galaxies only retain an average of 11% of the oxygen generated by their stars. The remaining oxygen likely escapes into space during powerful supernova explosions. This finding indicates that smaller galaxies have greater difficulty retaining their materials than previously believed. Researchers plan to conduct further studies to examine where this missing oxygen ultimately ends up. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Chinese scientists chill atoms to record low on Tiangong space station
item.description: Chinese scientists have chilled atoms aboard the Tiangong space station to the lowest temperature ever measured, smashing US and German records and paving the way for ultra-precise space sensors that could find hidden minerals, track climate change and test Einstein’s theory of gravity. Researchers from Peking University and the Chinese Academy of Sciences brought thousands of rubidium atoms, packed into a cloud smaller than a grain of sand, to less than 10 trillionths of a degree above absolute... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Ling Xin

item.title: Magnificent to observe Anil and Joshua getting ready to finalize their task.
item.description: Magnificent to observe Anil and Joshua getting ready to finalize their task. More power was definitely needed. And let's say a Big thanks to both of them.... Ver más Brenda Moira Eyre Magnificent to observe Anil and Joshua getting ready to finalize their task. More power was definitely needed. And let's say a Big thanks to both of them.... Ver más Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Blocking specific molecular signal on immune cells may restore ability to fight mutated cells
item.description: A previously unrecognized weakness in the immune defenses against certain blood neoplasms could offer a promising target for future treatments. Researchers have discovered that natural killer cells, which normally help the body eliminate malignant cells, remain remarkably active in patients with a particular genetic form of blood neoplasms. However, their ability to fight the disease appears to be restricted by an inhibitory molecular signal. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Controlling molecular helicity: A new approach to constructing chiral nanographenes
item.description: Nanographenes with up to eight helicene units can now be selectively synthesized using a two-step process. Researchers from Science Tokyo have developed a strategy to synthesize multi-helical nanographenes containing up to eight helicene units with controlled handedness. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: US study finds eating one avocado & mango every day improves blood vessel function in prediabetic adults
item.description: A new research study indicates that integrating mango and avocado into your daily diet may significantly improve heart health. Focused on adults with prediabetes, this study monitored the effects of these fruits over eight weeks with controlled calorie intake. Results showed enhanced blood vessel performance and lowered blood pressure in male participants, highlighting the cardiovascular advantages of incorporating these nutritious fruits into your meals. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Lifestyle Desk

item.title: Researchers explore how AI could improve earthquake safety
item.description: Researchers at the University of East London (UEL) have developed a new framework for assessing earthquake risks, using AI-assisted technology to examine how soil conditions, ground shaking and structural strength influence a building's ability to withstand seismic activity. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A well-timed blink helps us to look around
item.description: When did you last blink? Every few seconds, we briefly close our eyes, interrupting our view of the world. Most of the time, we do not notice. What is more, these brief interruptions hardly seem to interfere with our everyday activities. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: En 2007, EEUU tuvo la disparatada idea de fabricar cemento quemando montañas de alfombras viejas: el experimento funcionó, hasta que llegó la factura
item.description: Estados Unidos tenía un problema que se medía en millones de toneladas : cada año, una montaña de moquetas y alfombras usadas terminaba en los vertederos. En el año 2007, un grupo de investigadores encontró una salida tan extraña como prometedora: utilizarlas para alimentar los hornos de las cementeras. Lo sorprendente es que consiguieron demostrar que funcionaba. Lo que vino después fue una lección sobre la distancia que separa una buena idea de un negocio rentable. Millones de toneladas de alfombras. A comienzos de los años 2000, Estados Unidos generaba anualmente entre 1,8 y 2,3 millones… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Coating made from renewable plant-based materials could simplify recycling while reducing exposure to microplastics
item.description: The lining in traditional disposable coffee cups can release plastic particles and be difficult to recycle, but a new plant-based coating can eliminate these issues with your morning brew. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New European database to support environmental risk assessment of human pharmaceuticals
item.description: The PREMIER project, a public-private European consortium of research organizations (like Radboud University) and international pharmaceutical companies, has launched a new database to support the environmental risk assessment (ERA) of human pharmaceuticals. The data is publicly accessible, free of charge. The database was built with key user requirements in mind. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A sweeter future? AI helps scientists discover new sugar substitutes
item.description: Researchers Dr. Shayma El-Atawneh and professor Amiram Goldblum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem have developed a new computational framework that identified 92 promising candidates for future sugar substitutes from more than 50 million chemical compounds. The study, published in the journal Food Chemistry, demonstrates how artificial intelligence and molecular modeling could accelerate the discovery of new sweeteners while helping overcome one of the industry's persistent challenges: unwanted bitter aftertastes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: After 40 years of searching, physicists find evidence for an ultrarare particle decay
item.description: Physicists at CERN report that they've detected evidence of a rare meson particle decay (B⁰→ µ⁺µ⁻) that occurs when the meson's beauty quark annihilates with a down-type quark. The pair decays into a muon and antimuon, which are particles similar to electrons. Because evidence for this decay helps test theoretical predictions from the Standard Model, physicists have been waiting for it since 1984, when it was first theorized. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Study suggests there is no 'right' way to teach statistics, giving flexibility to educators
item.description: A new study has investigated whether challenges faced by educators in teaching statistics could be reduced by changing how it is taught. The findings suggest there is no single "right way," giving educators flexibility to choose how best to teach the subject. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Tiny animal populations can recover, challenging assumptions about extinction risk
item.description: Species reduced to fewer than 50 individuals in the wild are not automatically doomed to extinction, according to a major study co-authored by researchers at the Zoological Society of London and Monash University. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The way media reports suicide can help save lives
item.description: The way the media reports suicide can be important. It can bring an often-silenced issue into public view and draw attention to the social conditions that may have contributed to a death. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Mystery origin of iconic Stonehenge Altar Stone deepens as search narrows
item.description: The hunt for the source of Stonehenge's mysterious Altar Stone has entered a new phase after scientists ruled out several previously proposed locations and moved a step closer to identifying its origins. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Research supports communitywide efforts to fight bedbug infestations, expert explains
item.description: Rather than being a poverty problem, bedbugs are actually everyone's problem. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How do octopuses remember? Scientists uncover a surprising secret
item.description: How does an octopus remember what it has learned? A new study led by Dr. Ana Luiza Turchetti-Maia, Dr. Tal Shomrat and professor Binyamin (Benny) Hochner—researchers from the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Ruppin Academic Center—has uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that may help explain how these remarkably intelligent animals form and maintain memories. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Too many e-scooters? Blame competition
item.description: In 2018, something strange happened on sidewalks across America. In 65 cities, thousands of electric scooters appeared seemingly overnight, often with little or no advance notice to local governments. Cease-and-desist orders flew. Scooters were impounded. Even after cities imposed regulations, there seemed to be far more scooters than anyone could ever use. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A 70-million-year-old genetic rescue allowed codfishes to escape extinction and shape the North Atlantic
item.description: A new study has revealed how the repurposing of an ancestral gene saved the embryos of cod's ancestors from extinction, enabling them to form the large populations that, millions of years later, would change the course of human history. The codfishes and their relatives in the order Gadiformes lost genes essential for egg buoyancy and the survival of their embryos, yet survived by adaptively recruiting mechanisms that aid egg ovulation in freshwater fishes. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Plagiarism is a kind of theft, but it is also a question of honor
item.description: Any concept that has a history, philosopher Michel Foucault tells us, cannot have a fixed definition. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Archaeologists uncover possible 19th-century castaway camp on island 'at the end of the world'
item.description: On a desolate island at the end of the world, battered by freezing winds, archaeologists have uncovered the remains of a possible 19th-century castaway camp that may have belonged to a renowned Argentine sailor and his shipwrecked crew. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When Einstein's gravitational waves meet Newton's tides
item.description: Newton's theory of gravity has described the tides accurately for centuries. But could a tiny trace of Einstein's general relativity also be hidden in them? In a new study, a mathematician at Freie Universität Berlin has outlined how a targeted approach could be used to search for effects of this nature. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA's Swift telescope has burned up, months after a robot sent to save it failed
item.description: NASA's Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory took its last look at the sky on Oct. 20, 2026, while orbiting about 171 miles (275 kilometers) above Earth. NASA ended the telescope's mission three days later, because Swift had sunk so low that drag from the thin air there meant its telescopes couldn't hold steady. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australian classrooms are getting a 'digital detox'—what does this mean for schools and students?
item.description: The federal government is pushing for a "digital detox" in schools. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth's slowing spin may have shaped its primordial crust
item.description: Around 4.5 billion years ago, a planet-sized object collided with the newly formed Earth, throwing out the debris that would later form the moon. The collision left Earth spinning extremely fast, with days lasting just two to five hours. Yet existing models of how Earth's first crust formed and evolved have largely overlooked how the planet's later slowdown might have affected it. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Midwestern City Lights
item.description: City lights from the Midwestern United States to the East Coast sparkle across the landscape a couple of hours before sunrise on Oct. 18, 2026. Major urban areas visible in the photograph include Chicago, Illinois; Detroit, Michigan; and the New York metropolitan region. The International Space Station was orbiting 259 miles above Earth when this […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: HQ Web Team

item.title: NASA Astronauts to Answer Questions from Florida Students
item.description: Students in Florida will hear from NASA astronauts Jessica Watkins and Luke Delaney as they answer prerecorded STEM questions while aboard the International Space Station. The Earth-to-space call will begin at 10:40 a.m. EST Tuesday, Nov. 10, and will stream live on the agency’s Learn With NASA YouTube channel. This event is hosted by Freedom Crossing Academy in […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Gerelle Q. Dodson

item.title: From doctors and teachers to lawyers, every profession has a duty to align with climate goals
item.description: A Dutch family doctor named Tibor Poelmann posted a petition on an online forum for general practitioners (GPs) in 2021. He wanted their pension fund to stop investing in oil and gas. It quickly gathered 1,200 signatures. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Coordinated activity gives large pedestrian crowds a distinctive seismic signature
item.description: Large pedestrian crowds generate distinctive seismic signals depending on their collective behavior, according to a new study that includes data from Tokyo schools and outdoor gatherings in the United States and Israel. These seismic signals are strongest in the 1–2 hertz frequency band, which is consistent with human walking frequencies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Young children like sharks, but fear grows with age
item.description: Most young children like sharks, with almost seven in 10 describing them in a positive light, but a new study has found that associations between sharks and fear become more common as children get older. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Which infinity is bigger? Under alternative mathematical rules, a 2D map emerges
item.description: It is one of the great questions of mathematics: What does "infinity" actually mean? Which infinities are larger than others? Can infinities be arranged in a sequence, like the rungs of an endless ladder, so that for any two of them we can always say which one lies above the other? Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: New statistical method eliminates AI estimation bias in econometrics
item.description: A new research paper describes a statistical framework that resolves significant calculation biases caused by artificial intelligence in econometric models. The method, two-step extraction, removes estimation bias when researchers measure the business or economic effects of variables extracted using machine learning algorithms from unstructured data such as photos and consumer text. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Webb Space Telescope's little red dots could hold key to first black holes
item.description: Johns Hopkins researchers searching the expanse of the universe for the existence of the first black holes are zeroing in on little red dots that may hold the key to the theoretical phenomenon. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Swiss Army knife of the Hawaiian Islands—how an endangered bird drills into trees to find food
item.description: There are no woodpeckers on the Hawaiian Islands, but a little yellow bird called the 'akiapōlāʻau (Ah-key-ah-pole-ah-ow) has evolved an unusual beak to drill into branches to find food. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A clever molecular trick unlocks previously impossible properties in glass
item.description: Scientists have discovered how to reprogram the internal structure of glass using a special molecule that rearranges chemical bonds while lowering the melting temperature. The breakthrough could unlock entirely new glass materials with precisely controlled magnetic and optical properties, opening possibilities for advanced electronics, sensors, and other technologies. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: 400,000-year-old teeth reveal a stunning twist in human evolution
item.description: A groundbreaking discovery is rewriting the story of human evolution, revealing that an ancient human species once thought to be an evolutionary dead end may have left genetic traces in people alive today. By extracting proteins from 400,000-year-old Homo erectus teeth discovered in China, scientists uncovered evidence suggesting that these early humans interbred with Denisovans, another mysterious ancient human group. That genetic connection may have eventually reached modern populations in the Philippines, Papua New Guinea, and other parts of Southeast Asia. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Hubble Learns Galactic History From Stars
item.description: This Hubble image features the sparkling collection of stars named Messier 30 (M30), also called NGC 7099. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Scientists discover mysterious “lonely” brain waves linked to memory loss
item.description: Scientists have uncovered a surprising link between Alzheimer’s-related protein buildup, disrupted brain waves during deep sleep, and fading memory. The findings suggest that hidden changes in how the brain processes memories overnight may contribute to age-related memory loss long before Alzheimer’s symptoms appear. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Goodbye, cavities? Scientists create gel that could regrow tooth enamel
item.description: Scientists have developed a revolutionary gel that could regrow lost tooth enamel by harnessing minerals naturally found in saliva, potentially overcoming one of dentistry’s biggest limitations. The regenerated enamel behaves much like healthy enamel, raising hopes for a simple treatment that could repair damaged teeth, prevent decay, and reduce sensitivity. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Scientists solve 30-year-old mystery and discover a hidden defense against inflammation
item.description: Scientists have solved a decades-old mystery and uncovered a hidden immune system defense that protects healthy cells from the very inflammation meant to fight infections. The surprising discovery could lead to new approaches for treating cancer, inflammatory bowel disease, and other conditions involving excessive inflammation. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: El telescopio Swift ya es historia: se ha desintegrado sobre Sumatra tras 22 años en órbita
item.description: La NASA hizo todo lo posible para rescatar el Observatorio Neil Gehrels Swift de una caída inevitable. El pasado mes de julio, después de detectar que la reentrada del observatorio espacial era casi inminente, se lanzó la misión Link, cuyo objetivo era sujetar el telescopio e impulsarlo a una órbita más estable. Desgraciadamente, la nave que debía hacerlo sufrió una serie de problemas que la llevaron de vuelta a casa sin cumplir con su propósito. Por eso, como cabía esperar, el Swift ha acabado cayendo en la Tierra sin que nadie pudiese evitarlo. Ocurrió este miércoles, 4 de noviembre, en… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Azucena Martín

item.title: En 2021, unos científicos tuvieron la idea absurda de enseñar a las vacas a ir al baño. 10 días después no daban crédito a lo que veían
item.description: Enseñar a una vaca a utilizar un retrete parece una ocurrencia propia de una comedia. Sin embargo, en 2021, un equipo de investigadores de Alemania y Nueva Zelanda decidió comprobar si era posible . Lo que descubrieron en apenas diez días no solo puso en cuestión lo que creíamos saber sobre la inteligencia de estos animales, sino que abrió una vía inesperada para reducir la contaminación de las granjas. Una idea que parecía imposible. Durante décadas, los científicos habían asumido que el ganado bovino apenas controlaba cuándo y dónde orinaba. A diferencia de otros animales, como los perros… Fuente: Xataka.
item.dc:creator: Miguel Jorge

item.title: Fractal patterns reveal hidden limits to AI predictability
item.description: Researchers at the University of Sydney have identified a fundamental mathematical reason why artificial intelligence systems can learn different behaviors even when trained under almost identical conditions, a discovery that could help improve the reliability and trustworthiness of AI technologies. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Prehistoric 'giant rat' found in Thailand from fossil teeth
item.description: A giant rodent weighing around 30 kilograms (66 pounds) roamed what is now southern Thailand 33 to 35 million years ago, scientists said, after identifying a previously unknown species from two fossilized teeth. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Australia launches A$28 million project to stop invasive cane toads from reaching Pilbara after 1935 introduction
item.description: A new project involving Curtin University and Rio Tinto seeks to establish a waterless barrier for cane toads. The initiative intends to protect Western Australia's Pilbara area from the ecologically damaging species. Researchers plan to modify water sources over a significant area to prevent the toads' survival. Traditional Owners have been engaged throughout the project to ensure cultural significance is respected. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Australia approves seabed site where a Japanese company will store carbon pollution
item.description: Australia has designated a seabed storage site near its northern coast where a Japanese company plans to store massive amounts of carbon pollution using a technology that has divided climate scientists. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA astronauts cast US election votes from the International Space Station
item.description: In a rare event, three American astronauts voted in Tuesday's US midterm elections from the International Space Station, using advanced links to send electronic ballots to officials on Earth. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: ‘Zeptoverse’: CERN scientists uncover evidence of extraordinarily rare particle decay
item.description: Scientists at CERN have found evidence of an extraordinarily rare particle decay using the Large Hadron Collider. The process is predicted to occur just once in every 10 billion cases, offering researchers a new way to explore the subatomic world. Fuente: Euronews.

item.title: Bandicoot research uncovers new subspecies amid conservation calls
item.description: Researchers say new discoveries about bandicoot species could have conservation implications for South Australian populations of the marsupials. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Clem Stanley

item.title: NASA’s 3,200-pound Swift space telescope crashes back to Earth over Indonesia after failed $30 million rescue mission
item.description: NASA’s Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory re-entered Earth's atmosphere after 22 years in orbit, ending its mission. Swift was crucial for understanding gamma-ray bursts and other cosmic events, detecting over 2,000 bursts. The spacecraft's orbit deteriorated due to increased solar activity, leading to its uncontrolled descent. NASA attempted a rescue operation, but it ultimately failed, resulting in its re-entry on November 4, 2026. Fuente: The Times of India - World.
item.dc:creator: TOI Science Desk

item.title: Cyprus: Island of Snakes, Cats, and Ophiolites
item.description: The third-largest island in the Mediterranean Sea exposes an ancient piece of the ocean floor and hosts a clowder of cats. Fuente: NASA.

item.title: Centuries-old cemetery helps scientists link climate shocks to Industrial Revolution disease
item.description: During England's Industrial Revolution, when the country's farming-based economy transformed into an industrial one between roughly 1760 and 1840, pollution, harsh working conditions, inadequate housing and limited access to sunlight drove disease. Rickets, in which the growing skeleton fails to properly mineralize, was commonplace among children. Traditionally, urbanization, latitude and socioeconomic status were considered the main drivers. A factor that has largely been overlooked is climate. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A tiny supercurrent could unlock quantum information without destroying it
item.description: Researchers have proposed a breakthrough technique for reading quantum information without destroying the delicate states that make quantum computers work. By detecting an electrical signal generated by the qubit itself, their method achieved up to 99.85% accuracy in simulations and could make future quantum computers simpler and more efficient. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Why so many British pubs are closing down
item.description: British pubs are disappearing at an alarming rate. Last year, around eight closed down every week. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists turn viruses into weapons against deadly superbugs
item.description: Scientists are advancing a promising new way to fight antibiotic-resistant infections by using viruses that specifically target and kill harmful bacteria. An international team has released the first coordinated guidelines for personalized phage therapy, offering a roadmap for safely bringing this experimental treatment into clinical practice. Early findings are encouraging, with one study reporting improvement in 77% of patients and the disappearance of targeted bacteria in 61%. Fuente: ScienceDaily.

item.title: Thriving koala population near major NSW city could be chlamydia-free
item.description: Chlamydia poses a deadly threat to koalas, but researchers believe they have found a disease-free population near Newcastle. Fuente: ABC News Australia.
item.dc:creator: Laurise Dickson

item.title: NASA Announces X-70 Experimental Aircraft to Advance Flight Research
item.description: On Wednesday, NASA unveiled its newest experimental aircraft, the X-70 Fractal, during the UP.Summit at the agency’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. This high-performance, highly adaptable research platform is designed to accelerate the development and testing of advanced aviation technologies. The crewed X-70 features advanced, rapidly reconfigurable flight-control technology that will allow NASA to explore […] Fuente: NASA.
item.dc:creator: Cheryl Warner

item.title: Japan's ALS community is ready to become research partners, nationwide survey suggests
item.description: People living with ALS and their families in Japan are eager to help shape research on the disease, even though most have never heard of patient and public involvement (PPI), according to a study published on Oct. 30, 2026, in Research Involvement and Engagement. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: A new route to calculating gluon production in proton–nucleus collisions
item.description: In the theoretical study of proton-nucleus collisions, the colliding projectiles can be described as streams of color charges moving along their respective trajectories. These color charges couple to gluons, which then produce the particles that are observed in the final state (gluons and quarks, which eventually produce hadrons). Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Earth atmosphere emulators could enable faster and more accurate weather predictions
item.description: If you partitioned the entire Earth, from just below the surface to the top of the atmosphere, into 1-kilometer-square chunks, there would be billions of them. Now run each of those cells through a series of complex physics equations, and you can see how the entire Earth system interacts and evolves in detail, one step at a time. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: European orbiter detects fresh hints of volcanic activity on Mars
item.description: New evidence from gas seeping above volcanic rifts suggests Mars is not geologically dead deep inside, but merely sleeping. Fresh fissures along the Alba Mons region hint at active spots under the surface, where gases from inside the planet may be making their way up to the surface. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: How ranchers on Brazil's 'Dirty List' bypass forced labor safeguards by selling cattle through intermediaries
item.description: Brazil's "Dirty List," a public registry that names employers found to have violated anti-slavery laws, is a key component of the country's efforts to combat forced labor. Major meatpackers in Brazil signed sustainable sourcing commitments promising to not purchase cattle directly from ranchers on the Dirty List. But new research shows that ranchers have found ways around these restrictions, rerouting cattle through intermediaries and allowing cattle linked to forced labor to remain in domestic and international beef and leather supply chains. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: First direct observations reveal hydrogen dissolved in tiny gaps between metal atoms
item.description: University of Sydney researchers have made a breakthrough by directly observing hydrogen in the tiny spaces between the atoms in metal alloys. The world-first observation of hydrogen dissolving in these 'metal crystal lattices' offers fresh insights into why hydrogen can weaken metals and how more hydrogen-resistant materials might be developed. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Scientists reveal how cosignaling receptors dually regulate T cell activation via phase separation
item.description: Previous studies have shown that upon antigen stimulation, the T cell receptor (TCR) undergoes phase separation with the kinase Lck to mediate rapid T cell activation. However, the manner in which costimulating receptors regulate this process has remained unclear. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Ancient coins suggest influential Iron Age king was female
item.description: Bournemouth University (BU) archaeological research has revealed that Iron Age British ruler "Verica," who was central to the Roman invasion of Britain in A.D. 43, was in fact a woman. This discovery rewrites the history of early Roman Britain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: When customers cross the line: Study reveals hidden toll of harassment on gig workers
item.description: A rideshare driver picks up a passenger who makes repeated unwanted sexual comments. The ride ends, but the experience doesn't. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: The hidden cost of flexible work in academia: women do more parenting
item.description: Nature, Published online: 05 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03568-0 Policies designed to keep women in the workforce could be entrenching gendered parenting roles. Fuente: Nature.
item.dc:creator: Rachel Fieldhouse

item.title: Using ChatGPT at work? Your boss may trust you less, new study finds
item.description: Artificial intelligence may be making employees faster and more productive, but it could also be quietly damaging their careers. A new study led by Samuel Meyers, a Ph.D. student, together with his adviser Dr. Yochanan Bigman of the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and Dr. Roman Briker of WHU—Otto Beisheim School of Management in Germany, suggests that workers who use ChatGPT and other AI tools may pay an unexpected professional price: their managers are less likely to trust them. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Nasa’s 22-year-old Swift satellite telescope falls from orbit in fiery finale
item.description: Nasa’s Swift satellite ⁠telescope, which spent two decades studying the most powerful known blasts of energy in the cosmos, tumbled out of orbit as expected on Wednesday and burned up in Earth’s atmosphere over Indonesia, the space agency reported. The fiery demise of the Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory, weighing roughly 3,200 pounds (1,452kg), came less than three months after a ‌rescue spacecraft failed its mission to boost the satellite to higher orbit and extend its life. The US Space Force... Fuente: South China Morning Post.
item.dc:creator: Reuters

item.title: Entrepreneurs who struggle to understand their emotions are less committed to their business goals, study finds
item.description: Entrepreneurs who struggle to recognize and make sense of their own emotions are less likely to feel attached to their businesses and less committed to achieving their goals, particularly in high-stress periods, according to new research from the University of Bath School of Management. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Genetic interaction map could lead to better antibiotic pairings for tuberculosis
item.description: Rockefeller scientists have created the most comprehensive map to date of how essential genes interact in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), the bacterium responsible for tuberculosis (TB). The unprecedented map reveals thousands of previously unknown genetic relationships, offering a new window into the inner workings of one of the world's deadliest pathogens. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA Swift telescope plummets to Earth over Indonesia
item.description: NASA's Swift telescope has re-entered Earth's atmosphere near Sumatra in Indonesia following a failed rescue attempt earlier this year. Fuente: ABC News Australia.

item.title: A carefully timed pair of light pulses can amplify the motion of atomic layers in a quantum material
item.description: The principle "Work smarter, not harder!" apparently also applies to controlling quantum materials with light. Many of their fascinating properties depend on how the atoms are arranged in the crystal. Ultrashort laser pulses can be used to alter these structures in a targeted way—the light first excites electrons, whose changed energy and dynamics exert forces on the atomic nuclei and can thereby set the atoms in motion. Such processes unfold within femtoseconds, a millionth of a billionth of a second. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: NASA navigation experiment shows promise for planetary landings
item.description: NASA has successfully demonstrated technology designed to help spacecraft autonomously navigate to safe landing sites on the moon and on other planets. An Alta-X drone equipped with the agency's Safe and Precise Landing—Integrated Capabilities Evolution (SPLICE) guidance, navigation and control payload completed simulated lunar descent and landing maneuvers Aug. 27. The flight took place at Rogers Dry Lake near NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center in Edwards, California. Publicado también por: NASA. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Flat feet may have helped Neanderthals stay stable while carrying heavy loads
item.description: In all likelihood, the Neanderthals had flat feet. But it was not a defect at all. Instead, it was the consequence of a precise functional strategy to reduce impact stress under heavy loads and maximize stability on mountainous or rough terrain. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Hundreds of Ice Age rock art engravings discovered hidden in plain sight
item.description: Archaeologists have discovered the third-largest assemblage of Ice Age cave art ever found in Mediterranean Iberia in a region thought devoid of cave art, transforming our knowledge of Paleolithic European art. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: Trust in influencers grows more important in predicting buying intentions over time, analysis finds
item.description: A meta-analysis of empirical studies involving more than 31,000 participants has revealed the factors that affect the level of influence of so-called social media influencers. Those factors include credibility, expertise, attractiveness and perceived similarity to their followers. They are, the work shows, positively associated with the attitude of consumers toward the brands mentioned or promoted by those influencers and, in turn, their purchasing intentions. Details of the analysis are published in the International Journal of Internet Marketing and Advertising. Fuente: Phys.org.

item.title: What was really behind Wednesday's monster rally? Trump quickly making peace
item.description: The stock market skyrocketed after a decisive sweep for Democrats in the 2026 midterm elections, a move that Trump's reaction added to. Fuente: CNBC - World.

item.title: Carbon dots fluoresce their way through the rainbow as liquids change
item.description: Fluorescent materials usually emit a single consistent color. They are typically made from dyes or metallic components. In contrast, researchers reporting in ACS Central Science have created carbon dots that can fluoresce in a range of colors under UV light, depending on the concentration and the liquid they're in. The team incorporated the new carbon dots into plastic decorations and used them to create a data encryption system. Fuente: Phys.org.
